To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the relationships between conformity to specific masculine norms (i.e., playboy, selfreliance, risk-taking, and violence) and psychological distress differ in specific groups of males.

(1) a 2-class latent class solution was optimal in terms of explaining differential associations between conformity to the masculine gender norms and psychological distress, and (2) the 2 classes of men differed in the specific associations between conformity to these norms and psychological distress.

(a) the optimal number of classes that best explained the differential relationships between conformity and psychological distress in our sample was 2 and (b) the 2 classes were characterized by different patterns of relationships between conformity and distress, and the classes were associated with age and race/ethnicity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how different groups of men experience the relationship between conformity to masculine ideals and psychological distress.
the question of how are specific dimensions of masculine norms related to psychological distress among different groups of men?
the relationship between conformity to masculine gender norms and men's psychological distress.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

men who are detached risk-takers (i.e., men who are high in playboyism, self-reliant, and risk-taking and low in violence and conformity to traditional masculine norms) are more likely to experience psychological distress than men who are risk avoiders (i.e., low in playboyism and risk-taking and high in conformity to traditional masculine and violence norms).
the association between masculine norms and psychological well-being is complex and multifaceted, and that the association may differ by age and race/ethnicity.
there are different groups of men with differential associations between conformity to the masculine role and psychological distress.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the associations between masculine norms and psychological health are complex, and that these associations are moderated by men's social context and identity.

the associations between conformity to specific masculine norms and psychological well-being are not universal across men but are contingent upon men's social location and psychological characteristics.
there is a need to examine the relationship between masculinity and psychological distress in specific subgroups of men.
The main takeaway from our work is that

men who are high on the masculine norms of risk-taking, self-reliant, and playboy are at risk for psychological distress, whereas men who are high only on the masculine norm of playboy are not at risk.
the associations between masculinity and distress are not uniform across all groups of men.

men who are more conforming to the masculine norm for risk-taking are less likely to be distressed, but men who are conforming to masculine norms of playboys, self-reliant, and risk-taking are more likely to be distressed.
